passages.heading: Description
passages.source: Los Alamos National Laboratory, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.text: It is the only liquid that cannot be solidified by lowering the temperature. It remains liquid down to absolute zero at ordinary pressures, but will readily solidify by increasing the pressure.

passages.heading: History
passages.source: Jefferson Lab, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.text: The first recorded use of a fluorine compound dates to around 1670 to a set of instructions for etching glass that called for Bohemian emerald (CaF2).

passages.heading: History
passages.source: IUPAC Commission on Isotopic Abundances and Atomic Weights (CIAAW)
passages.text: It was discovered in hydrofluoric acid by the Swedish pharmacist and chemist Carl-Wilhelm Scheele in 1771, but it was not isolated until 1886 by the French pharmacist and chemist Henri Moissan.

passages.heading: History
passages.source: Los Alamos National Laboratory, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.text: The ancient Greeks and Romans used alum as an astringent and as a mordant in dyeing.

passages.heading: History
passages.source: IUPAC Commission on Isotopic Abundances and Atomic Weights (CIAAW)
passages.text: In 1825, the Danish physicist, Hans Christian Oersted, isolated impure aluminium.

passages.heading: History
passages.source: IUPAC Commission on Isotopic Abundances and Atomic Weights (CIAAW)
passages.text: Amorphous silicon was discovered by the Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius in 1824. Crystalline silicon was first prepared by the French chemist Henri Sainte-Claire Deville in 1854.

passages.heading: History
passages.source: Los Alamos National Laboratory, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.text: Though lime was prepared by the Romans in the first century under the name calx, the metal was not discovered until 1808.

passages.heading: History
passages.source: Jefferson Lab, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.text: Metallic calcium was first isolated by Sir Humphry Davy in 1808 through the electrolysis of a mixture of lime (CaO) and mercuric oxide (HgO).

passages.heading: Uses
passages.source: Jefferson Lab, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.text: When heated at standard atmospheric pressure, arsenic changes directly from a solid to a gas, or sublimates, at a temperature of 887 K. In order to form liquid arsenic, the atmospheric pressure must be increased. At 28 times standard atmospheric pressure, arsenic melts at a temperature of 1090 K.

passages.heading: History
passages.source: Jefferson Lab, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.text: A total of 0.05 micrograms (0.00000005 grams) of astatine have been produced to date.

passages.heading: Uses
passages.source: Jefferson Lab, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.text: Due to the small amounts produced and its short half-life, there are currently no uses for astatine outside of basic scientific research.

passages.heading: History
passages.source: Los Alamos National Laboratory, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.text: No weighable quantity of the element has been prepared or isolated.

passages.heading: Uses
passages.source: Jefferson Lab, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.text: Due to the small amounts produced and its short half-life, there are currently no uses for francium outside of basic scientific research.

passages.heading: Description
passages.source: Los Alamos National Laboratory, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.text: Fermium is the heaviest synthetic element that can be formed by neutron bombardment of lighter elements, and hence the heaviest element that can be prepared in macroscopic quantities.

passages.heading: Description
passages.source: Los Alamos National Laboratory, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.text: Fermium metal has not been prepared, however measurements have been made on fermium alloys with rare earth metals and a number of predictions have been made.

passages.heading: Uses
passages.source: Jefferson Lab, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.text: Due to the small amounts produced and its short half-life, there are currently no uses for fermium outside of basic scientific research.

passages.heading: Uses
passages.source: Jefferson Lab, U.S. Department of Energy
passages.text: Since only small amounts of mendelevium have ever been produced, it currently has no uses outside of basic scientific research.
